Well, I... I suppose I'm here because things have just gotten too heavy. My sister actually drove me, but I came in because I just keep thinking, every single night when I finally lay down, that it would just be so much better if I didn't wake up. Like, if the morning just didn't happen for me and I could just slip away in my sleep. It wouldn't just be easier, it would be right. 

I do flooring for a living—tile, carpet, a lot of hard labor on your knees all day, you know? I work with a really good crew. Or, I used to. But lately, I just... I feel like dying would be the fair punishment for what I've done to my family and my crew. I've just completely ruined everything for them, brought all this down on them, and I can't fix it. I can't go to the job sites, I can't face the guys, I can't look my family in the eye. I can't do anything but lay there and think about how my being dead is the only way to make it right. It's just this constant, heavy loop in my head that I deserve to be punished, that not waking up is the only fair price for the damage I've caused everyone who relies on me. So I just lay there, hoping my heart just stops so they can finally be free of me.

No, no, I really don't. It's funny you ask that, because I used to be such a... I don't know, a vibrant person? I used to do so much. Before my husband got hurt, before all this guilt just started eating me alive, I had a whole life outside of the flooring jobs. I used to paint, for one. Watercolors, mostly. I'd set up my easel in the sunroom on Sunday mornings and just get lost in the colors for hours. I loved mixing them, watching how they bled into the paper. And cooking—oh, I used to cook these huge, elaborate meals for the two of us, or even invite the crew over for a big barbecue on the weekends. I'd spend all day prepping, marinating, baking from scratch. It was my way of showing love, I guess.

I even did community theater! I know, a tile installer doing theater, it sounds silly, but I loved it. I never missed a rehearsal, I knew all my lines, I loved the energy of being on stage.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, yeah, I have... I've definitely lost weight. It's not like I'm trying to, though. I mean, who tries to lose weight when everything else is falling apart? But my clothes... my work pants, especially. I have these heavy-duty canvas pants that I used to wear to the job sites, you know, with the reinforced knees for all the tile work. I put them on the other day—just to see if I could even still fit into my old life, I guess—and they were just hanging off me. I had to pull my belt in three notches past where it used to sit, and even then, they looked baggy. It's like I'm just shrinking away.

And it's because I just... I don't eat. I forget. Or, it's not even that I forget, it's that the thought of food just doesn't even register most of the time. I'll wake up—if you can call it waking up—and the whole day will just blur past me. The sun goes down, and I'll realize I haven't had a single thing since the day before. And when my sister comes over and forces me to eat, or if I finally realize my stomach is cramping and I try to force down some toast or a few bites of whatever she brought... I just feel sick. Like, physically nauseous. I'll take two bites and my throat just closes up. It feels like my body is rejecting it, like I don't even deserve the nourishment, you know? Like I'm being punished from the inside out. So yeah, the weight is just falling off because I can't bring myself to eat more than a few bites before I feel like I'm going to throw up. It's just... it's just another thing that's fading away.

I... well, yes. I didn't want to tell anyone about this because I know how it sounds, but yes, I have. It's actually really terrifying, to be honest with you. It started happening a while ago, and it's always this... this man's voice. 

I'll be in my kitchen, right? And my kitchen is this tight little galley style, so it's narrow, with the fridge at one end by the back door and the sink right under this little window that looks out into the side yard. I'll just be standing there, maybe staring out the window, not even doing anything, just frozen and stuck in my head like I usually am these days. And suddenly, right behind my shoulder—usually my left shoulder—I'll hear him. 

It's not a whisper, and it's not like a thought in my head, if that makes sense. It's loud and clear, exactly as if a real, physical person has snuck up right behind me and is standing inches away. He says things like, "You missed it." Or he'll say, "Everyone knows." And the tone... it's so deep and cold and accusatory. It sends this horrible chill right down my spine, all the way to my tailbone. I whip around, my heart just pounding out of my chest, fully expecting to see a man standing right there on the linoleum, but the kitchen is completely empty. The back door is locked and deadbolted. There is absolutely no one there. 

And it's not just at home, either. It used to happen at the job sites, back when I was still trying to force myself to work. I remember this one specific time, I was laying this ceramic subway tile in a client's master bathroom. It was this huge, echoing room with these awful vaulted ceilings, and I was on my knees, troweling the thinset onto the wall, just trying to focus. And then I heard it. Same voice. Right behind me. "Everyone knows." I dropped my trowel and spun around so fast I nearly knocked over my whole bucket of mortar. I was ready to yell at whoever had sneaked up on me. But it was just me. Just me and the tile. The homeowner wasn't even home, the house was completely empty. 

But I heard him. I swear to you, doctor, I heard him as clearly as I hear you speaking to me right now. It's driving me out of my mind because I know nobody is there when I turn around, but the voice is so incredibly real. How can it be so real if the room is empty? It just... it feeds right into that horrible guilt I was telling you about. It's like this invisible person is just following me around, confirming every single awful thing I already feel about myself, and I can't make him stop.

Yeah... I mean, yes, I do. It's actually really frustrating because in my head, everything makes perfect sense, but when it comes out of my mouth, people just look at me like I'm speaking a different language. 

Like, for example, back when I was still trying to work, if someone—maybe my sister or a client—asked me to explain what happened on a job, or why a project was taking so long. I'll start trying to explain it to them, right? And I'll start talking about the tile lines, because you have to get the grout lines perfectly straight, especially if you're working with those large-format porcelain tiles, otherwise the whole room just looks entirely crooked and the eye goes right to the mistake. But then, just thinking about lifting those heavy tiles makes my brain jump straight to my husband's back brace. You know, the heavy black one with the rigid metal stays in the back that he had to wear after he threw his back out unloading the work truck that one time, and how the velcro on it was always getting full of lint and wearing out. 

And then, just from thinking about that brace, my mind automatically jumps over to the license paperwork. Because I remember we had to file the contractor license renewal and all the liability insurance forms right around the exact same time he hurt his back, and the city was being so incredibly difficult about the permits for that specific job... 

And before I know it, I'm talking about the permit office downtown and the lady behind the glass, and whoever I'm talking to will just stop me. They'll hold up their hands and tell me I'm not answering the question. They'll say, "What does any of this have to do with the bathroom floor?" And it just makes me feel so... broken, I guess. Because to me, it's a perfectly straight line. The tile lines, the back brace, the paperwork... it all feels completely connected in my head. It's all part of the exact same story, the exact same memory, and I don't understand how they don't see how it all links together. But I guess to everyone else, my thoughts are just jumping all over the place and making no sense at all. So, yeah, it is really hard to keep track, because I feel like I'm giving all the necessary details to paint the whole picture, but nobody else can follow the thread.

It wouldn't just be easier, it would be right. \n\nI do flooring for a living—tile, carpet, a lot of hard labor on your knees all day, you know? I work with a really good crew. Or, I used to. But lately, I just... I feel like dying would be the fair punishment for what I've done to my family and my crew. I've just completely ruined everything for them, brought all this down on them, and I can't fix it. I can't go to the job sites, I can't face the guys, I can't look my family in the eye. I can't do anything but lay there and think about how my being dead is the only way to make it right. It's just this constant, heavy loop in my head that I deserve to be punished, that not waking up is the only fair price for the damage I've caused everyone who relies on me. So I just lay there, hoping my heart just stops so they can finally be free of me.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been having these thoughts about not waking up and feeling like you deserve to be punished?\n\nPatient: Well, it's... it's been a long time. It feels like forever, honestly, but if I really think about it, sit down and trace it back... it's been about a year and two months. Yeah, a year and two months of this... this crushing weight. It started a few months after my husband's injury. He got hurt, and at first, I was just running on adrenaline, you know? Just trying to keep the house afloat, keep the bills paid, keep working my jobs. I was doing tile in this huge commercial building downtown, working ten, sometimes twelve-hour days, coming home, taking care of him, doing everything. \n\nBut then, a few months after it happened, when things were supposed to be settling into a routine, that's when it just... it fell on me. The darkness, I mean. It just settled over me like a thick, heavy blanket and it hasn't lifted since. A year and two months of waking up—when I do manage to sleep—and just immediately feeling that dread, that absolute certainty that I am the problem. I can remember the exact week it started getting really bad, too. It was right around the time the leaves started changing last year, and I remember looking out the window of the truck on the way to a job site and thinking, 'I shouldn't be here. I don't deserve to be here.' And it's just been every single day since then. Fourteen months of just... waiting for the end, because the guilt is just so loud.\n\nDoctor: Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy before these thoughts started?\n\nPatient: No, no, I really don't. It's funny you ask that, because I used to be such a... I don't know, a vibrant person? I used to do so much. Before my husband got hurt, before all this guilt just started eating me alive, I had a whole life outside of the flooring jobs. I used to paint, for one. Watercolors, mostly. I'd set up my easel in the sunroom on Sunday mornings and just get lost in the colors for hours. I loved mixing them, watching how they bled into the paper. And cooking—oh, I used to cook these huge, elaborate meals for the two of us, or even invite the crew over for a big barbecue on the weekends. I'd spend all day prepping, marinating, baking from scratch. It was my way of showing love, I guess.\n\nAnd I used to be so active, too. I'd go for a three-mile run every single morning before I even strapped on my knee pads for work. It cleared my head, got me ready for the day. I even did community theater! I know, a tile installer doing theater, it sounds silly, but I loved it. I never missed a rehearsal, I knew all my lines, I loved the energy of being on stage. \n\nBut now... now it's all just gone. The easel has been folded up in the closet for over a year. The paint tubes are probably dried out. If I even think about cooking, it just feels like this insurmountable mountain of effort. We eat frozen dinners, or my sister brings food, because the thought of chopping an onion just... it drains whatever tiny bit of energy I have left. I haven't run a single step, and the theater group actually called me a few times when I stopped showing up, but I just ignored the calls. I just didn't care. I still don't care. All those things... painting, cooking, running, the plays... they feel like they belong to somebody else entirely. Like chores from a life I don't even recognize anymore. I just can't bring myself to care if I miss out on them, because honestly, I don't think I deserve to enjoy them anyway. I just sit there and think about how I shouldn't be allowed to have fun when everything is so broken.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're moving more slowly than you used to, or that it takes you longer to do things?\n\nPatient: Well, I... I don't know if I'm moving slower, exactly. I mean, maybe? I haven't really paid attention to how long it takes me to do things because I'm just not doing much of anything at all. Like I said, I'm not going to the job sites, I'm not running, I'm not cooking. I just lay there. So I don't really have a good way to measure if I'm moving slower than I used to. \n\nI guess when I do have to get up, like to go to the bathroom or if my sister forces me to come sit in the living room while she's here, it feels like... like walking through water, maybe? But I don't know if that's because my body is actually moving slower or if it's just that the weight of everything is so heavy that it feels like it takes a massive amount of effort just to put one foot in front of the other. It's like my limbs are filled with lead, you know? But as for actually timing myself or noticing if it takes me twenty minutes to do something that used to take five... I really couldn't tell you. I'm just so stuck in my own head, in that loop of knowing I've ruined everything, that I don't really notice what my physical body is doing most of the time. I'm just... existing, barely. So, I don't know. I'm not sure.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past year?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, I have... I've definitely lost weight. It's not like I'm trying to, though. I mean, who tries to lose weight when everything else is falling apart? But my clothes... my work pants, especially. I have these heavy-duty canvas pants that I used to wear to the job sites, you know, with the reinforced knees for all the tile work. I put them on the other day—just to see if I could even still fit into my old life, I guess—and they were just hanging off me. I had to pull my belt in three notches past where it used to sit, and even then, they looked baggy. It's like I'm just shrinking away.\n\nAnd it's because I just... I don't eat. I forget. Or, it's not even that I forget, it's that the thought of food just doesn't even register most of the time. I'll wake up—if you can call it waking up—and the whole day will just blur past me. The sun goes down, and I'll realize I haven't had a single thing since the day before. And when my sister comes over and forces me to eat, or if I finally realize my stomach is cramping and I try to force down some toast or a few bites of whatever she brought... I just feel sick. Like, physically nauseous. I'll take two bites and my throat just closes up. It feels like my body is rejecting it, like I don't even deserve the nourishment, you know? Like I'm being punished from the inside out. So yeah, the weight is just falling off because I can't bring myself to eat more than a few bites before I feel like I'm going to throw up. It's just... it's just another thing that's fading away.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever heard voices or seen things that other people couldn't hear or see?\n\nPatient: I... well, yes. I didn't want to tell anyone about this because I know how it sounds, but yes, I have. It's actually really terrifying, to be honest with you. It started happening a while ago, and it's always this... this man's voice. \n\nI'll be in my kitchen, right? And my kitchen is this tight little galley style, so it's narrow, with the fridge at one end by the back door and the sink right under this little window that looks out into the side yard. I'll just be standing there, maybe staring out the window, not even doing anything, just frozen and stuck in my head like I usually am these days. And suddenly, right behind my shoulder—usually my left shoulder—I'll hear him. \n\nIt's not a whisper, and it's not like a thought in my head, if that makes sense. It's loud and clear, exactly as if a real, physical person has snuck up right behind me and is standing inches away. He says things like, \"You missed it.\" Or he'll say, \"Everyone knows.\" And the tone... it's so deep and cold and accusatory. It sends this horrible chill right down my spine, all the way to my tailbone. I whip around, my heart just pounding out of my chest, fully expecting to see a man standing right there on the linoleum, but the kitchen is completely empty. The back door is locked and deadbolted. There is absolutely no one there. \n\nAnd it's not just at home, either. It used to happen at the job sites, back when I was still trying to force myself to work. I remember this one specific time, I was laying this ceramic subway tile in a client's master bathroom. It was this huge, echoing room with these awful vaulted ceilings, and I was on my knees, troweling the thinset onto the wall, just trying to focus. And then I heard it. Same voice. Right behind me. \"Everyone knows.\" I dropped my trowel and spun around so fast I nearly knocked over my whole bucket of mortar. I was ready to yell at whoever had sneaked up on me. But it was just me. Just me and the tile. The homeowner wasn't even home, the house was completely empty. \n\nBut I heard him. I swear to you, doctor, I heard him as clearly as I hear you speaking to me right now. It just... it feeds right into that horrible guilt I was telling you about. It's like this invisible person is just following me around, confirming every single awful thing I already feel about myself, and I can't make him stop.\n\nDoctor: How often do you hear the man's voice?\n\nPatient: Well, it's... I’ll wake up, and for a split second, I might forget, but then I'm just waiting for it, my whole body just tense. \n\nLike I was just telling you about being in the kitchen or back when I was at the job sites... it happens so often that I'm constantly on edge, just waiting for that man's voice to come from right behind my shoulder. I'll start trying to explain it to them, right? But then, just thinking about lifting those heavy tiles makes my brain jump straight to my husband's back brace. Well, yeah, that's exactly what I was just trying to explain to you with the whole... the whole thing about the bathroom tile and my husband's back brace. That's exactly it. 

It's like... people think I'm going off-topic, right? They think I'm just wandering away from the point or that I can't focus. If someone asks me a simple question, they expect this simple, straight-line answer. But in my head, it doesn't work like that. The topic isn't just one tiny little box. I have to explain the tile lines, because the tile lines are the foundation, and that heavy lifting directly connects to the back brace, which directly connects to the license paperwork we were filing at the exact same time. 

So when you ask if I have trouble sticking to one topic... to me, I *am* sticking to the topic! It is all one topic. It’s all one big, connected web in my brain. But my sister, or whoever I'm talking to, they'll just cut me off right in the middle of me explaining it. They'll hold up their hands and just sigh and say, "Can you please just stick to the point?" And I'm sitting there, just completely deflated, thinking, I *am* sticking to the point! How do you not see that the back brace and the permit office are the exact reason the job went the way it did? 

It’s so incredibly exhausting trying to talk to anyone these days. I feel like I have to explain every single detail so they can understand the full picture of what I'm saying, but they just lose patience with me. They just tell me I'm not answering the question, even though I'm giving them all the answers, all the context they could possibly need. It makes me want to just stop talking to people altogether, to be honest with you, because what is the point of even opening my mouth if nobody is willing to follow along with how everything is connected?

High in mood? Like... really energetic? No. No, never. I mean, I honestly don't even know what that would feel like, to be honest with you. 

Even on my absolute best days, even years ago before everything got so incredibly heavy and complicated... I was never one of those people who just bounces off the walls or feels on top of the world. You have to understand, my line of work—installing carpet, laying down tile, hauling boxes of porcelain and those massive, heavy rolls of carpet padding up and down flights of stairs all day—it just drains every single ounce of energy out of you. It is completely physical, back-breaking work. You come home and your knees are throbbing, your hands are completely raw and calloused from using the carpet kicker, and the dust is just settled deep into your skin. So the idea of having "extreme energy" or feeling "extremely high" in mood... it just doesn't even compute for me. 

Even during that brief window I was just telling you about, when I felt a little lighter and started making myself toast in the mornings again? That wasn't a high. That wasn't extra energy. That was just... baseline. That was just me finally scraping together barely enough energy to exist like a normal human being for a few hours. I have never felt elated, or like I could take on the world, or like my mind was racing with all these amazing, happy ideas. It's always just been this constant, exhausting push to get through the day, to get the room measurements right, to deal with the suppliers and the clients without collapsing. 

So, no. I've never had a period like that. I honestly wish I did have a little extra energy sometimes, just to get through the day-to-day things like the laundry or the billing paperwork, but no... never anything extreme or high like you're talking about. Just tired. Always just tired.

Well, "plot" makes it sound like some kind of spy movie, but... yes. Absolutely yes. It’s all connected. And the thing is, doctor, this isn't just some passing thought I have when I'm feeling really low. Like, I'll be mapping out a complex herringbone layout, or even just a standard one-third offset for wood-look plank tile, and I can see how the boxes were left in the room by the delivery guys, or how the chalk lines on the subfloor were marked before I even got there. It’s a grid. It's a way of boxing me in and watching me. 

And then there are the texts from the suppliers. You'd think a text saying my mortar is ready for pickup or that a certain grout color is on backorder is just a normal message, right? But it's not. The timing of it, the specific wording they use... it coordinates perfectly with exactly what I'm doing in that exact moment. And the permit calls! The homeowners will stand out in the hallway and pretend they're just calling the city to check on the inspection schedules or the plumbing permits, but I know they're actually calling to log my hours, to report back on whether I'm intentionally sabotaging their bathrooms or messing up the transitions. 

People try to tell me I'm overthinking it. People who don't work in the trades, they try to tell me that a text from a supplier is just a text, or that the homeowner is just anxious about their remodel. But no one can talk me out of it. They can talk until they're blue in the face, but I know what I'm seeing. I know what's happening. I've been doing this too long to miss the signs. They are meticulously tracking whether I'm ruining these jobs on purpose, and that voice I hear? He’s just the narrator for the whole sick operation, making sure I know they're watching. So yes, it's a plot. It’s a massive, coordinated effort, and it just never, ever stops.

Separate. Oh, it's definitely separate. I mean, if it were just my own mind, it would sound like my own thoughts, wouldn't it? Like when you're thinking to yourself about what groceries you need, or when I'm calculating the square footage and the waste factor for a complex tile layout in my head. It is a man's voice. A very distinct, physical man's voice coming from right behind me. And it doesn't even stop when I leave work. It happens at home, too, right in my own kitchen when I'm just trying to make a cup of coffee and feeling too heavy to even lift the mug. He'll just speak, right over my shoulder, saying things like, "You missed it," or "Everyone knows." 

And it is so loud and so incredibly clear, doctor. It is exactly as if a living, breathing person is standing mere inches away from my neck. I can almost feel the air move, you know? It's that real. So of course, my first instinct is always to whip around. I'll drop my trowel on the subfloor, or I'll spill my coffee on the counter, and I spin around expecting to see one of the general contractors who snuck up on me, or a delivery guy, or... or someone who broke into my house to monitor me. But... there's absolutely nobody there. Just empty space. An empty room or an empty kitchen. I'll search the whole house, check the locks, look out the windows, and there is no one. 

So no, there is no way my own mind could project something that sounds that external. If it was my mind, I wouldn't be turning around to look for the person attached to the voice. It's him. Like I said, he's the one narrating this whole sick operation they're running on me, and he is very much a separate thing, outside of my own head, making sure I know they've got me cornered.

They want to destroy my livelihood and my reputation. \n\nI've thought about this a lot, doctor, lying awake at night, just turning it over and over in my head. Why me? Why go through all this trouble with the floor patterns and the supplier texts? And it's because they want to catch me in a lie. They want to prove that I'm incompetent, that I'm a fraud, that I'm doing a terrible job on purpose. They want to strip away everything I've worked for. I've been doing this for over fifteen years. I started as an apprentice right after I dropped out of college, carrying buckets of thinset that weighed more than I did, ruining my knees before I was even thirty. I built a reputation as someone who does clean, precise work. And now... now they want to take all of that and twist it.\n\nSo, are they out to harm me? Yes, in a way that matters more than just a punch in the face. They want to expose me, humiliate me, and probably make sure I never work again. And the voice... the man's voice, he agrees. He tells me they're right to do it, that I deserve to be exposed because I'm a failure anyway. So it's not just that they're tracking me, it's that they're building a case. A massive, undeniable case against me. And honestly, the anticipation of when they're finally going to drop the hammer and take everything away... it's exhausting. It's just so exhausting.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe the voice you're hearing is trying to communicate a specific message to you or is it just random?\n\nPatient: Well, it's definitely not random. Not at all. It feels incredibly specific, like it's aimed right at the core of me. It’s a man’s voice, and he’s not just babbling nonsense or making background noise. He has these very specific things he says, and they always tie right into whatever I'm doing or whatever I'm terrified of in that moment. \n\nFor instance, I'll be at a job site, right? I'll be down on my hands and knees, maybe smoothing out the adhesive or trying to get the grout lines perfectly straight—because, like I was saying before, if they aren't straight, I know they'll use it against me. So I'm down there, hyper-focused, and right behind me, just right over my shoulder, I'll hear him say, \"You missed it.\" Just like that. Or I'll be at home, off the clock, just standing in my own kitchen trying to make a cup of coffee or staring at the sink, and the voice will come from right behind me and say, \"Everyone knows.\" \n\nAnd I mean, doctor, it is so incredibly clear. It's not like a thought echoing in my head, or like a memory, or the wind, or the pipes settling in the house. It sounds exactly like a physical, living, breathing human being is standing inches away from the back of my neck. It’s so real and so loud that every single time it happens, my heart just jumps right up into my throat and I whip around. I'll drop my trowel on the floor, or I'll spill my coffee on the counter, and I spin around fully expecting to see a man standing right there in my kitchen or on the job site. I brace myself for it. \n\nBut... when I turn around, nobody's there. It's just empty space. Just the cabinets, or the unfinished drywall. But the message itself? Yes, the message is very clear and very specific. He wants me to know that I'm failing, that I've missed something important, and that everyone is completely aware of what a fraud I am. It's this deliberate, targeted commentary, and it just never really stops.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the people who you believe are tracking you are trying to hurt you physically or just damage your reputation?\n\nPatient: I mean... I think I just went over this, doctor. Like I was just explaining a minute ago, it's not a physical thing. They aren't trying to beat me up or, you know, push me down a flight of stairs at a job site or something. Why would they even need to? My body is already completely wrecked from this job anyway. If you spend fifteen years on your knees scraping up old linoleum and laying down heavy ceramic tile, your back and your joints are already destroyed, so physical pain isn't really the ultimate threat here. \n\nNo, it's... it's exactly what I was just saying, it's my reputation. It's my entire livelihood. In the flooring business, especially around here where all the general contractors talk to each other at the supply houses... reputation is literally everything. If word gets around that you're sloppy, or worse, that you're intentionally sabotaging a layout—like if you mess up the grout lines on a custom master bathroom floor that some homeowner just paid ten thousand dollars for in materials alone—you are completely done. You will never get another bid. \n\nAnd that is exactly what they want. They want to completely dismantle my name. They want to make it so that when someone asks a supplier about me, all they hear is that I'm a complete fraud who ruins properties. It's so much worse than physical harm, because physical harm heals, you know? A broken arm heals, a cut heals. But if they convince the whole city that I'm incompetent and malicious, I lose everything I've spent my entire adult life building since I left college. And honestly, with how incredibly heavy and dark everything feels lately, with me barely able to even drag myself out from under the covers most mornings... I don't have the energy to fight them on it. I just don't. They know I'm weak right now, they know I'm struggling just to exist, and they're using that exact timing to destroy my name. So yeah, like I said, it's not my body they're after. It's my whole life.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe the voice you're hearing and the feelings of being watched are part of a plot against you?\n\nPatient: Well, \"plot\" makes it sound like some kind of spy movie, but... yes. Absolutely yes. It’s all connected. And the thing is, doctor, this isn't just some passing thought I have when I'm feeling really low. I know I've talked about how heavy everything gets, how I spend days just completely paralyzed by it. But even when that lifts a little? Even when I'm not crying or down in bed, and I actually have the energy to stand up and go to a site, this... this reality doesn't change. I get absolutely certain—I mean, I *am* certain—that the homeowners and the suppliers are all in on it together. \n\nThey have this whole elaborate system to track me, to monitor every single move I make to see whether I'm ruining their jobs on purpose. Like, I'll be mapping out a complex herringbone layout, or even just a standard one-third offset for wood-look plank tile, and I can see how the boxes were left in the room by the delivery guys, or how the chalk lines on the subfloor were marked before I even got there. It’s a grid. It's a way of boxing me in and watching me. \n\nAnd then there are the texts from the suppliers. You'd think a text saying my mortar is ready for pickup or that a certain grout color is on backorder is just a normal message, right? But it's not. The timing of it, the specific wording they use... it coordinates perfectly with exactly what I'm doing in that exact moment. And the permit calls! The homeowners will stand out in the hallway and pretend they're just calling the city to check on the inspection schedules or the plumbing permits, but I know they're actually calling to log my hours, to report back on whether I'm intentionally sabotaging their bathrooms or messing up the transitions. \n\nPeople try to tell me I'm overthinking it. People who don't work in the trades, they try to tell me that a text from a supplier is just a text, or that the homeowner is just anxious about their remodel. But no one can talk me out of it. They can talk until they're blue in the face, but I know what I'm seeing. I know what's happening. I've been doing this too long to miss the signs. They are meticulously tracking whether I'm ruining these jobs on purpose, and that voice I hear? He’s just the narrator for the whole sick operation, making sure I know they're watching. So yes, it's a plot. It’s a massive, coordinated effort, and it just never, ever stops.\n\nDoctor: How long have you believed that people are tracking you and trying to ruin your reputation?\n\nPatient: Let me think... because time just sort of blurs together lately with how exhausted I am, but... if I really trace it back, look at my job logs and my invoices from last year... it’s been right around eleven months. It was this huge residential remodel over in the Heights—a massive master bath, all natural stone, tumbled travertine. That's when I realized the way their text messages about my mortar orders or my backordered Schluter strips were suddenly syncing up perfectly with whatever I was doing in that house. So it’s been eleven solid months of this. Eleven months of the voices, eleven months of knowing without a shadow of a doubt that they are tracking my every move through these jobs and these messages, just waiting for me to slip up so they can destroy my reputation. \n\nAnd, I mean, you try living like that for almost a year, doctor. You try waking up every single day for eleven months, dragging yourself out of bed when your body hurts and your mind is just so impossibly dark and heavy, only to go to a job site where you know the homeowners and the delivery guys have set up a grid to monitor you. It just... it wears you down to absolute nothing. You can't even look at your phone without knowing it's part of the system. But yes, to answer your question, it's been about eleven months of the voices and the tracking.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe the voice you're hearing is a part of your own mind or something separate from you?\n\nPatient: Separate. Oh, it's definitely separate. I mean, if it were just my own mind, it would sound like my own thoughts, wouldn't it? Like when you're thinking to yourself about what groceries you need, or when I'm calculating the square footage and the waste factor for a complex tile layout in my head. You know what your own inner voice sounds like. But this... this is completely different. \n\nIt is a man's voice. A very distinct, physical man's voice coming from right behind me. It happens all the time at the job sites, like I was saying earlier, when I'm down on my hands and knees measuring out a layout or spreading thinset, just trying to push through the exhaustion. And it doesn't even stop when I leave work. It happens at home, too, right in my own kitchen when I'm just trying to make a cup of coffee and feeling too heavy to even lift the mug. He'll just speak, right over my shoulder, saying things like, \"You missed it,\" or \"Everyone knows.\" \n\nAnd it is so loud and so incredibly clear, doctor. It is exactly as if a living, breathing person is standing mere inches away from my neck. I can almost feel the air move, you know? It's that real. So of course, my first instinct is always to whip around. I'll drop my trowel on the subfloor, or I'll spill my coffee on the counter, and I spin around expecting to see one of the general contractors who snuck up on me, or a delivery guy, or... or someone who broke into my house to monitor me. But... there's absolutely nobody there. Just empty space. An empty room or an empty kitchen. I'll search the whole house, check the locks, look out the windows, and there is no one. \n\nSo no, there is no way my own mind could project something that sounds that external. If it was my mind, I wouldn't be turning around to look for the person attached to the voice. It's him. Like I said, he's the one narrating this whole sick operation they're running on me, and he is very much a separate thing, outside of my own head, making sure I know they've got me cornered."
